entities.name: Ibn Hud
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abū ’Abd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf ibn Hūd al-Judhamī, commonly known as Ibn Hud, emerged as a pivotal, albeit ultimately unsuccessful, figure in 13th-century al-Andalus, leading a decade-long resistance (1228–1238) against the encroaching Christian Reconquista. Claiming direct descent from the Hudid dynasty that had ruled the Taifa of Zaragoza until 1118, Ibn Hud capitalized on the profound power vacuum left by the collapsing Almohad Caliphate, attempting to forge a unified Muslim front across a vast expanse of the Iberian Peninsula. His efforts, spanning from Murcia to Seville, represented the last significant, large-scale attempt to re-establish a widespread Muslim domain before the final consolidation of Christian kingdoms.

Ibn Hud's ascent began in Murcia in 1228, where he orchestrated a popular revolt against the Almohad governor, quickly gaining support across al-Andalus. Within months, he controlled major cities including Córdoba, Seville, Granada, Málaga, and Jaén, effectively recreating a substantial taifa emirate. Despite initial military successes against local Almohad remnants, his reign was characterized by relentless pressure from the Christian kingdoms of Castile and Aragon. He lost strategic territories such as Baeza in 1227 (predating his major rise but indicative of the Christian advance) and, most significantly, the ancient Caliphal capital of Córdoba to Ferdinand III of Castile in 1236, a devastating blow that signaled the irreversible decline of Muslim power.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ibn Hud's decade-long rule represented the last major, large-scale attempt to unify Muslim al-Andalus against the Christian Reconquista, directly preceding the final collapse of widespread Muslim power and the emergence of the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada as the sole survivor.
